screens.title: Variables, Data Types, and Basic Input/Output
screens.narratorSegment: In game development, every change in state—player health, position, or whether a door is open—relies on storing data in memory. This lesson introduces variables as named storage locations and the core data types C++ gives you to represent those values: integers for counts and scores, floating point numbers for positions and velocities, characters for single symbols, and booleans for binary states. You will see how to declare and initialize variables, use constants to protect values that must not change, and perform arithmetic including addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and modulo. We also cover console input and output so your program can ask for a player name or numbers and print results. Along the way I’ll point out common pitfalls you will meet early on, such as uninitialized variables, integer division truncation, and simple type mismatches. By the end you’ll be able to pick appropriate types for game values and write small interactive programs that read input, compute results, and display meaningful output.

screens.title: What is a Variable?
screens.narratorSegment: A variable is a named location in memory that holds a value your program can read or change. Think of it like a labeled box where the label is the variable name and the box has a size decided by the data type. In a game, variables represent player health, enemy counts, positions, and boolean flags such as whether a gate is open. The type tells the compiler how many bytes to reserve and how to interpret those bits. For example, an int will reserve a whole-number representation while a float will allow fractional values. A concrete example: storing a player's score as an int makes sense because scores are whole numbers, but storing coordinates typically uses float because fractional values matter. A common misconception is that a variable can safely be used immediately after declaration; in C++ uninitialized variables contain garbage and should be initialized. As a takeaway, always consider the meaning of the data you'll store, pick a type that matches that meaning and initialize the variable to a predictable starting state. What is a Variable? means variable = named, typed memory; choose type by the value's nature and initialize to avoid undefined contents.. In practical terms, a concrete definition and why it matters in games. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › What is a Variable?
Definition

Variable as named storage

A variable binds a name to a value and allocates memory sized by its type. This binding lets your code read and write game state predictably when initialized correctly.

Analogy
Imagine labeled boxes for health, score, and position. If a box is empty you cannot rely on its contents—initialize it before use.
Example
int playerScore = 0; // a labeled box starting at zero
Misconception
Declaring without initializing leaves unpredictable data in that memory location.
Visual: variable anatomy
Name
Label you use in code
Type
Determines size and interpretation
Value
The current data stored in memory
Key Takeaway

Always choose a type that matches the data's nature and initialize variables to prevent undefined behavior.

screens.title: Declaring and Initializing Variables
screens.narratorSegment: Declaring a variable consists of specifying its type and name, and optionally giving it an initial value. In C++ a common pattern is 'type name = value;'. Initialization avoids undefined contents and documents intent. For example, writing int enemyCount = 5; both declares enemyCount and sets it to five. You can also declare and assign later, but delaying initialization risks using garbage. Use const for values that must never change; const float PI = 3.14159f; communicates intent and prevents accidental modification. A practical gotcha is the float literal suffix: 100.0f indicates a float literal, while 100.0 is a double. Mixing them without awareness can cause implicit conversions. Another useful pattern is zero-initialization for counters and flags. For arrays and structs, consistent initialization reduces bugs. Always verify that the initial value makes sense for gameplay: starting health should not exceed maximum health, counters start at zero, booleans default to false when appropriate. These simple patterns make code safer and easier to reason about. Declaring and Initializing Variables means declare with a clear initial value; use const for invariants and choose literal suffixes to match type.. In practical terms, syntax, examples, and safe patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Declaration & Initialization
Process

Declare, then initialize or initialize immediately

Choose one of these safe forms and prefer initializing at declaration to avoid undefined values.
Pattern 1 — Declare & Initialize
int playerScore = 0; // recommended for counters and scores
Pattern 2 — Declare then assign
int enemyCount; enemyCount = 5; // allowed, but riskier if read before assign
Pattern 3 — Constant
const float MAX_HEALTH = 100.0f; // prevents accidental change
Key Takeaway

Prefer initialization at declaration and use const for values that must not change.

Common examples
<!-- Code panel --> 
#include <iostream>

int main() {
  int playerScore = 0;
  float playerHealth = 100.0f;
  bool isGameOver = false;
  const int MAX_PLAYERS = 4;

  // Later in code
  playerScore += 10;
  return 0;
}
Note: using the 'f' suffix on 100.0f indicates a float literal. Without it the literal is double and may be implicitly converted.

screens.title: Integer Types: int, short, long, unsigned
screens.narratorSegment: Integers store whole numbers and come in several sizes: short, int, long, and long long. The exact byte size varies by platform, but the key idea is range. Use int for most game counters like score, enemy count, or level number because it balances range and performance. Use short when memory is extremely constrained and values stay small; use long long when you expect very large totals. The unsigned modifier removes negative values and doubles the positive range, which is useful for totals that can never fall below zero, such as inventory counts or cumulative points. However, unsigned arithmetic can be surprising when mixing signed and unsigned types because implicit conversions may change results, so prefer explicit casts when needed. A concrete example: unsigned int totalCoins is safe when coins never go negative, but subtracting a larger signed value can underflow. The takeaway: pick a size that fits the expected range and be mindful of signedness when mixing types. Integer Types: int, short, long, unsigned means use int by default; choose short/long only when range or memory justify it; use unsigned for strictly non-negative counts but handle conversions carefully.. In practical terms, when to use each integer type in game code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Integer Types
Comparison

int vs short vs long vs unsigned

int
Default choice for counters and scores. Balance of range and performance.
short / long
Use only when memory or range needs demand it; long long for very large totals.
unsigned
For strictly non-negative values. Beware of underflow when subtracting.
Mixing types
Implicit conversions between signed and unsigned can yield surprising results; use explicit casts.
Concrete scenario
Use int for enemyCount and score. Use unsigned for inventory slots if you are confident values remain non-negative. If totals may grow enormous, choose long long.
Example & warning
// Example
int score = 100;
unsigned int coins = 50;
// Subtracting signed value from unsigned can underflow
int penalty = 75;
coins = coins - penalty; // careful: unsigned underflow possible
Check your arithmetic and conversions when mixing signed and unsigned values; prefer explicit casts to document intent.

screens.title: float vs double
screens.narratorSegment: Floating-point types represent decimal numbers and come with trade-offs. float is single-precision and uses less memory; double is double-precision and offers much higher accuracy. In many game logic tasks like positions and velocities, float is sufficient and preferred because it uses less memory and can be faster on some hardware. Engine internals and physics systems sometimes favor double for accumulative precision in long-running simulations. A helpful concrete test is to accumulate small movements over many frames: using float can introduce small rounding errors that accumulate to visible drift, while double reduces that drift. However, double consumes more memory per value and may be slower in large arrays. A common misconception is that double is always better; in performance-sensitive code, the extra memory and cache pressure can harm overall performance. Choose float for large numbers of values where performance matters, and double when precision is critical and the data set is small or caching is not dominated by memory use. float vs double means use float for most game values for performance; use double selectively where rounding error must be minimized.. In practical terms, precision, memory, and when to prefer each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › float vs double
Comparison

Precision and performance trade-offs

Float uses less memory and is commonly used for positions, rotations, and per-vertex data. Double gives you more numeric precision which can be important for long-running accumulations or physics steps in engine code.
When to use float
Large arrays of coordinates, per-frame game logic, and when memory and cache are a priority.
When to use double
Critical engine calculations, physics integrators over long durations, or precise numeric tools.
Example test
// Accumulate small steps many times
float posF = 0.0f;
for (int i=0; i<1000000; ++i) posF += 0.0001f;

double posD = 0.0;
for (int i=0; i<1000000; ++i) posD += 0.0001;

// Compare final results to see drift
Run this loop to observe larger rounding drift in float than double. Use the result to decide which type fits your subsystem.

screens.title: char, bool, and const
screens.narratorSegment: The char type stores a single character value such as a letter, digit, or symbol, represented internally by an integer code like ASCII. Use char for single-key inputs or small text tokens, but for full strings you will use a string type covered later. The bool type holds true or false and is ideal for flags like isGameOver or hasKey; using bool makes intent explicit and helps readability. The const keyword declares a variable whose value cannot change after initialization. Constants are useful for fixed game parameters like maximum players or gravity. For example, const int MAX_PLAYERS = 4; signals an invariant and allows the compiler to enforce it. A common error is attempting to assign a new value to a const; the compiler will reject it. Another subtle point is char promotions in arithmetic: when you operate on chars they can be promoted to integers, so be mindful when mixing them with numeric operations. Use these small types for clarity and minimal memory when appropriate. char, bool, and const means use char for single characters, bool for binary state, and const to declare immutable values that document intent and prevent changes.. In practical terms, small types and protecting invariants. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › char, bool, const
Definition

Characters, booleans, and immutable values

Use char for single symbols; bool for true/false flags. Use const to protect values that must not change during execution.
char example
char initial = 'J'; // single letter stored as a small integer
bool example
bool hasKey = false; // true or false state for gameplay logic
const example
const float GAME_GRAVITY = 9.81f; // protects a constant game parameter
Pitfall & tip
Chars promote to ints in arithmetic. When mixing char with numeric operations, be explicit to avoid surprises. Use bool for binary logic rather than integers for clearer code.
Key Takeaway

Choose small types for clarity, and use const to declare invariants that document and enforce intent.

screens.title: Arithmetic Operators and Precedence
screens.narratorSegment: C++ supports standard arithmetic operators: addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and modulo for integer remainder. Operator precedence follows usual math rules: multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction, and parentheses override precedence. For reliable code, use parentheses to make intent explicit. A concrete example: 2 + 3 * 4 evaluates to 14 because multiplication runs first; writing (2 + 3) * 4 yields 20. The modulo operator returns the remainder of integer division and is useful for wrapping counters or determining odd/even values. Watch out for operator mixing between integers and floating-point types: the operation's result type depends on operand types, and integer division truncates decimals. Always test edge cases like division by zero and use conditional checks to guard operations where inputs may be zero. For game code, clarity and explicit grouping reduce bugs in calculations that affect movement, scoring, or physics. Arithmetic Operators and Precedence means remember precedence, use parentheses to document intent, and guard against division by zero and integer truncation.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Arithmetic & Precedence
Rule set

Order of evaluation and safe patterns

Multiplication and division before addition and subtraction. Use parentheses to express intent and avoid subtle bugs.
Example 1
2 + 3 * 4 evaluates to 14. To change order, use (2 + 3) * 4 which evaluates to 20.
Example 2 — Modulo
10 % 3 yields 1. Useful for wrapping indices and checking parity.
Guard division
Always check for zero in divisors to avoid runtime errors or undefined behavior.
Mini quiz
What does this evaluate to: int x = 5 + 2 * 3 / (1 + 1); Try computing step by step, respecting precedence and parentheses.
// Calculate step-by-step
int x = 5 + 2 * 3 / (1 + 1);
// (1 + 1) = 2
// 2 * 3 = 6
// 6 / 2 = 3
// 5 + 3 = 8
Use parentheses and comments when expressions become nontrivial to help reviewers and future you.

screens.title: Integer Division and Casting
screens.narratorSegment: Integer division discards any fractional part when both operands are integers. This is a frequent source of confusion: dividing 15 by 4 using integer operands yields 3, not 3.75. The result is computed as an integer before being stored, even if assigned to a floating-point variable afterwards. To obtain a fractional result you must ensure at least one operand is a floating-point type, either by using a float or double literal or by casting. For example, casting an integer to float before division yields a correct fractional value. Truncation and explicit casting

Code example
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
  // Declare and initialize
  float num1 = 0.0f;
  float num2 = 0.0f;

  std::cout << "Enter the first number: ";
  std::cin >> num1;

  std::cout << "Enter the second number: ";
  std::cin >> num2;

  float sum = num1 + num2;
  float difference = num1 - num2;
  float product = num1 * num2;
  float quotient = 0.0f;
  if (num2 != 0.0f) {
      quotient = num1 / num2;
  } else {
      std::cout << "Warning: Division by zero is not allowed." << std::endl;
  }

  // Remainder: cast to int for modulo
  int intNum1 = static_cast(num1);
  int intNum2 = static_cast(num2);
  if (intNum2 != 0) {
      int remainder = intNum1 % intNum2;
      std::cout << "Remainder: " << remainder << std::endl;
  }

  std::cout << "Sum: " << sum << std::endl;
  std::cout << "Quotient: " << quotient << std::endl;

  return 0;
}

In game development, every change in state—player health, position, or whether a door is open—relies on storing data in memory. This lesson introduces variables as named storage locations and the core data types C++ gives you to represent those values: integers for counts and scores, floating point numbers for positions and velocities, characters for single symbols, and booleans for binary states. You will see how to declare and initialize variables, use constants to protect values that must not change, and perform arithmetic including addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and modulo. We also cover console input and output so your program can ask for a player name or numbers and print results. Along the way I’ll point out common pitfalls you will meet early on, such as uninitialized variables, integer division truncation, and simple type mismatches. By the end you’ll be able to pick appropriate types for game values and write small interactive programs that read input, compute results, and display meaningful output.

These objectives map directly to practical tasks you will perform while learning C++ basics. First, you will declare and initialize variables using built-in types and see how initialization prevents unpredictable behavior. Second, you will learn the purpose and memory trade-offs of int, float, double, char, and bool, and when to use each in game contexts like scores, coordinates, and flags. Third, you will perform arithmetic operations and learn operator precedence, so your calculations match developer intent. Fourth, you'll use std::cin and std::cout to accept console input and display formatted results. Each objective is framed as a verifiable skill: writing a declaration, choosing a type, computing an expression, and constructing simple console interactions. These skills are foundational and will appear in debugging sessions and small tool development for games. Practice on short examples and check your outcomes against expected outputs to confirm competency.

A variable is a named location in memory that holds a value your program can read or change. Think of it like a labeled box where the label is the variable name and the box has a size decided by the data type. In a game, variables represent player health, enemy counts, positions, and boolean flags such as whether a gate is open. The type tells the compiler how many bytes to reserve and how to interpret those bits. For example, an int will reserve a whole-number representation while a float will allow fractional values. A concrete example: storing a player's score as an int makes sense because scores are whole numbers, but storing coordinates typically uses float because fractional values matter. A common misconception is that a variable can safely be used immediately after declaration; in C++ uninitialized variables contain garbage and should be initialized. Integers store whole numbers and come in several sizes: short, int, long, and long long. The exact byte size varies by platform, but the key idea is range. Use short when memory is extremely constrained and values stay small; use long long when you expect very large totals. C++ uses std::cout with the insertion operator to send text to the console and std::cin with the extraction operator to read values from the console. std::cout uses ' >' to extract values into variables and stops reading at whitespace. This means reading a player's name with std::cin will capture only a single word; for whole lines you need a different approach which we will cover later. Another common pitfall is that extraction fails when the input type does not match the variable type. New C++ programmers frequently encounter three recurring issues: uninitialized variables, type mismatches, and integer division surprises. Uninitialized variables contain whatever was in memory before; reading them yields unpredictable behavior. Always initialize variables when declaring them. Type mismatches occur when you mix types without explicit casts; implicit conversions can truncate or change values. Use static_cast to make conversions intentional and readable. Integer division truncation is another pitfall; remember that dividing two integers yields an integer result. Debugging tips: print variable values with std::cout to inspect intermediate results, and test edge cases like zero divisors or very large totals. When std::cin fails because of bad input, clear the stream and consume the invalid input before retrying. Here are three compact concepts to remember as you practice. First, a variable is a typed storage location; choose its type to match the data's nature and initialize it. Second, floats and doubles trade memory for precision—use float for performance when many values exist and double where precision accumulates noticeably. Third, input and arithmetic require care: use std::cin/std::cout for simple console input and output, guard divisions, and avoid integer division when a fractional result is intended. Keep these three rules in mind during coding and testing; they reduce bugs caused by incorrect assumptions about memory, precision, or input parsing.
